title: SAUL WAS READY TO KILL HIS OWN SON—AND THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN
paragraphs: SAUL WAS READY TO KILL HIS OWN SON—AND THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN

Jonathan had just helped save Israel. But instead of receiving his father's blessing, he was sentenced to death. What happened in 1 Samuel 14 exposes the frightening difference between defending God's honor and defending our own pride—and reveals why we desperately need Jesus Christ.
Imagine risking your life to save your people.
Imagine walking toward an enemy army with almost no chance of surviving, trusting God when everyone else is afraid.
Imagine watching the Lord turn an impossible situation into a victory.
Then imagine coming home and discovering that the person who wants you dead is your own father.
Not because you betrayed him.
Not because you joined the enemy.
Not because you rejected God.
But because you unknowingly broke a command you never heard.
And the man who gave that command would rather see you die than admit that he was wrong.
This is not a fictional tragedy.
This happened in the household of Israel's first king.
And the most disturbing part of the story is not simply that Saul threatened Jonathan's life.
It is that Saul was prepared to use the name of God to justify what he was about to do.
Read that again.
A man can speak passionately about God's honor while being dangerously protective of his own pride.
And before we condemn Saul too quickly, there is a question we need to confront.
Have we ever been so determined to prove ourselves right that we stopped caring whom we were hurting?
Because this story is not only about a king, a son, and a battlefield thousands of years ago.

It is about what happens when spiritual authority becomes entangled with insecurity, when religious zeal outruns obedience, and when someone mistakes the preservation of his reputation for the preservation of God's glory.
And somewhere in this ancient tragedy, there is a wounded son who deserved to be heard.
His name was Jonathan.
Before we reach the moment when Saul demanded his son's death, we need to understand what Jonathan had actually done.
Israel was facing the Philistines, an enemy whose military strength had left God's people in a frightening position.
Saul was king, but Jonathan was the one who stepped forward with extraordinary faith.
In 1 Samuel 14:6, Jonathan said to his armor-bearer:
"Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few." (KJV)
There is something breathtaking about that confession.
Jonathan did not claim to know exactly what God would do.
He did not pretend that faith eliminated danger.
He did not declare that victory was guaranteed because he felt courageous.
He simply understood something about the Lord that fear had caused others to forget.
God is not limited by the number of people standing beside you.
God does not require impressive resources before He can accomplish His purposes.
And faith does not always begin with certainty about the outcome. Sometimes it begins with confidence in the character of God.

Jonathan and his armor-bearer approached the Philistine outpost. The enemy challenged them to come up, and Jonathan understood the encounter as confirmation that the Lord had given the Philistines into Israel's hand.
They climbed toward the enemy.
The fighting began.
And God brought confusion and terror upon the Philistine forces.
The victory that followed was not merely the product of Jonathan's courage.
Scripture declares in 1 Samuel 14:23:
"So the LORD saved Israel that day." (KJV)
That sentence matters.
Jonathan was an instrument.
God was the Deliverer.
But while Jonathan was acting in faith, Saul had made a decision that would turn Israel's victory into a family crisis.
The king had placed his soldiers under a solemn oath.
"No one was permitted to eat until evening, until Saul had taken vengeance on his enemies."
The exact wording is revealing.
In 1 Samuel 14:24, Saul declared:
"Cursed be the man that eateth any food until evening, that I may be avenged on mine enemies." (KJV)
Notice those words.
"That I may be avenged."
The narrative does not explicitly tell us every motive hidden in Saul's heart. But his language places his own vengeance at the center of the command.
And the consequences were devastating.
The soldiers became faint from hunger.
The pursuit was hindered.
Later, the people's desperate hunger contributed to their eating meat with the blood, contrary to God's law (1 Samuel 14:32–33; Leviticus 17:10–14).
Saul's oath was not a command God had given to Israel.
It was an oath Saul imposed upon the army.
That distinction is essential.
Because not every command wrapped in religious language carries the authority of God.
Not every severe rule is evidence of holiness.
And not every leader who demands sacrifice is necessarily leading people in obedience to the Lord.
Sometimes human beings add burdens God never required.
And then they condemn others for failing to carry them.
Jonathan knew nothing about his father's oath.
He had been away when it was imposed.
During the pursuit, he came upon honey in the forest.
Exhausted from battle, he dipped the end of his staff into the honey and tasted it.
His strength returned.
The Bible describes it simply:
"His eyes were enlightened." (1 Samuel 14:27, KJV)
The Hebrew expression is striking:
וַתָּאֹרְנָה עֵינָיו — vattāʾōrnāh ʿênāyw
Literally, the expression conveys that his eyes became bright.
In context, it describes the visible renewal of Jonathan's vitality after eating.
He was hungry.
He ate honey.
His strength revived.
There was no secret rebellion.
No calculated insult toward his father.
No deliberate violation of a command he knew.
When someone informed Jonathan about Saul's oath, he recognized the damage it had caused.
"My father hath troubled the land." (1 Samuel 14:29, KJV)
Think about the weight of those words.
Jonathan was not rejecting God's authority.
He was recognizing the harmful consequences of his father's decision.
He understood that the army could have fought more effectively if the soldiers had been allowed to eat.
And this is where the story begins to expose a painful truth.
Sometimes the person accused of rebellion is the one who sees most clearly how badly things have gone wrong.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
Perhaps you grew up in a home where questioning an unfair decision was treated as disrespect.
Perhaps you served under someone who could never admit a mistake.
Perhaps you watched a leader demand loyalty while refusing accountability.
Perhaps you were told that keeping quiet was the same thing as honoring God.
And perhaps you have carried guilt for years because someone convinced you that disagreeing with them meant disagreeing with the Lord.
Jonathan's story does not teach us to despise authority.
Scripture repeatedly calls believers to honor legitimate authority and to practice humility.
But it does remind us that human authority is not infallible.
Even a king can be wrong.
Even a father can make a destructive decision.
Even someone speaking in the language of righteousness can act without wisdom.
And loyalty to God must never be confused with the unquestioning approval of everything a human leader does.
Then the story becomes even darker.
After the battle, Saul sought divine guidance about pursuing the Philistines further.
But he received no answer.
Saul concluded that sin must be present among the people and initiated a process to identify the offender.
The lot eventually fell upon Jonathan.
Here we need to read carefully.

The passage reports that Jonathan was identified through the casting of lots. It does not explicitly explain every reason God withheld an answer, nor does it declare that Jonathan deserved execution under God's law.
What it does show is Saul's response when his own son was identified.
In 1 Samuel 14:43, Saul asked Jonathan what he had done.
Jonathan answered:
"I did but taste a little honey with the end of the rod that was in mine hand, and, lo, I must die." (KJV)
There is something heartbreaking about that answer.
Jonathan did not invent an excuse.
He did not deny eating the honey.
He did not try to shift blame.
He acknowledged exactly what happened.
A little honey.
A staff.
An exhausted soldier.
An oath he had never heard.
And now death.
Can you imagine looking into your father's eyes, knowing that he has the power to spare you, and wondering whether his pride means more to him than your life?
Can you imagine the silence between them?
A son who had risked his life for Israel.
A father who had been given the responsibility to lead Israel.
One standing in the aftermath of a God-given victory.
The other standing before a decision that would reveal what he valued most.
Then Saul spoke the words that make this passage so terrifying.
"God do so and more also: for thou shalt surely die, Jonathan." (1 Samuel 14:44, KJV)
In Hebrew, the decisive declaration is:
כִּי־מוֹת תָּמוּת יוֹנָתָן — kî-môt tāmût yônātān
"Surely you shall die, Jonathan."
The Hebrew construction combines the infinitive absolute with the finite verb from the root מוּת (mût), meaning "to die."
This grammatical form intensifies the certainty of the declaration.
Saul was not merely expressing disappointment.
He was pronouncing a death sentence.
Against his own son.
And the opening of his statement invoked God in a solemn oath formula.
That is what makes the moment so chilling.
Saul's words sounded religious.
His decision was severe.
His determination appeared unshakable.
But religious intensity is not the same as spiritual faithfulness.
A person can be loud about righteousness and dangerously careless with mercy.
A person can defend a vow while ignoring the foolishness that produced it.
A person can become so consumed with maintaining authority that correction feels like humiliation.
And when that happens, other people often pay the price.
The Bible does not explicitly say Saul wanted Jonathan dead because he envied his victory. We should not add that motive to the text as though Scripture stated it.
But the narrative gives us sufficient reason to question Saul's judgment.
He imposed an oath that weakened the army.
He pursued its enforcement even after its harmful consequences became apparent.
And when the violation was traced to his own son, who had acted without knowing the oath, Saul insisted upon death.
His determination to uphold his pronouncement threatened to destroy the very son through whom God had worked.
Here is the frightening lesson.
When protecting our own decisions becomes more important than doing what is right, even the people we love can become casualties of our pride.
Some of the deepest wounds people carry did not come from strangers.
They came from someone whose love they trusted.
A father whose approval they desperately wanted.
A mother whose words they could never seem to satisfy.
A pastor whose correction became humiliation.
A spouse who used Scripture to win arguments instead of seeking truth.
A leader who demanded repentance from everyone except himself.
And the wounds become even more confusing when God's name is brought into the conflict.
Because how do you separate the character of a loving heavenly Father from the behavior of an earthly authority figure who has misrepresented Him?
How do you learn to trust God when someone used religious language to make you afraid?
How do you believe that grace is real when every mistake in your past was treated like a permanent sentence?
Jonathan's story speaks into that confusion.
It reminds us that the Bible does not hide the failures of its leaders.
God's Word does not ask us to pretend Saul was right simply because he was king.
It tells the truth.
And sometimes the beginning of healing is discovering that the wrong done to you was not a reflection of God's heart.
But the story does not end with Jonathan's sentence.
Something extraordinary happens.
The people intervene.
The same people who had endured Saul's exhausting oath now refuse to allow Jonathan to be killed.
In 1 Samuel 14:45, they say:

"Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: as the LORD liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he hath wrought with God this day." (KJV)
What a moment.
The soldiers had witnessed the victory.
They knew Jonathan had acted courageously.
They recognized God's work through him.
And they refused to remain silent while an unjust outcome unfolded before them.
The Hebrew text concludes with a remarkable statement:
וַיִּפְדּוּ הָעָם אֶת־יוֹנָתָן — vayyipdû hāʿām ʾet-yônātān
"So the people rescued Jonathan."
The verb comes from the Hebrew root פדה (pādâ), commonly associated with redeeming, ransoming, or delivering someone from danger or an obligation.
In this immediate context, it describes Jonathan being delivered from the threatened execution.
The text does not tell us that the people paid a monetary ransom.
It tells us that their intervention spared his life.
And then Scripture records the outcome:
"That he died not." (1 Samuel 14:45, KJV)
Four words.
But what a relief after everything that came before them.
He did not die.
The son was spared.
The king's death sentence was not carried out.
And the people who recognized God's work refused to confuse Saul's reckless oath with the righteousness of God.
Can you feel the emotional weight of that moment?
Jonathan had faced the Philistines and survived.
But now he had to be rescued from his own father's command.
The battlefield had not destroyed him.
The king's oath nearly did.
And sometimes that is how life feels.
You survive what everyone thought would break you.
You make it through the crisis.
You endure the loss, the betrayal, the sleepless nights, the struggle nobody knows about.
Then, just when you think the battle is over, the wound comes from somewhere you thought was safe.
And you begin to wonder whether God has forgotten you.
But Jonathan's deliverance reminds us that a human sentence does not automatically express the will of God.
The people recognized that the Lord had worked through Jonathan.
They stood against his execution.
And Jonathan lived.
Yet there is an even deeper reason this account belongs in the unfolding story of Scripture.
Because Jonathan's rescue, beautiful as it was, could not solve Israel's greatest problem.
The people had a king who could make destructive decisions.
They had a nation repeatedly struggling with disobedience.
They had hearts vulnerable to fear, pride, and self-justification.
And they needed more than a courageous prince.
They needed a righteous King.
That is where this story ultimately directs our attention toward Jesus Christ.
Not because Jonathan is a perfect or exact prophetic picture of Jesus.
He is not.
Jonathan was a courageous but finite human being, and his rescue was not an atoning sacrifice.
We must not force details of this historical account into symbolism that Scripture does not establish.
But when we read 1 Samuel within the larger biblical story, the contrast becomes powerful.
Saul was Israel's first king, and his failures exposed the limitations of sinful human leadership.
Jesus is the promised Son of David, the Messiah whose kingdom is righteous and everlasting.
Saul was willing to pronounce death upon his son to uphold his own oath.
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, willingly gave His own life in obedience to the Father to save sinners.
And the difference matters.
Jonathan was spared from death.
Jesus entered death voluntarily.
Jonathan was rescued by the intervention of the people.
Jesus gave Himself for the redemption of His people.
Jonathan's deliverance preserved one man's earthly life.
Christ's death and resurrection opened the way to forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life for everyone who believes in Him.
The Gospel is not that God overlooks evil because He is too kind to judge it.
The Gospel is that God is both just and merciful, and that Jesus Christ bore our sins in His own body on the cross.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we became spiritually impressive.
Not after we convinced everyone that we had never failed.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And here is where the story reaches beyond Jonathan.
Because some of us are not only wounded by people who behaved like Saul.
Sometimes we have behaved like Saul ourselves.
We have demanded perfection while excusing our own failures.
We have spoken harshly when we should have listened.
We have refused to apologize because admitting fault felt unbearable.
We have used our positions, our experience, or even our knowledge of Scripture to win battles we should have surrendered to God.
We have wounded people while telling ourselves we were simply defending what was right.
And the Holy Spirit may be bringing someone to mind right now.
Someone you embarrassed.
Someone you silenced.
Someone whose explanation you refused to hear.
Someone who needed your compassion but received your anger.
Someone who stopped opening up to you because every conversation became a trial.
The question is not whether you can find a verse to justify being severe.
The question is whether your actions reflect the truth, humility, justice, and love revealed in Jesus Christ.
If this is exposing something in your heart, do not rush past it.
You do not have to defend what God is calling you to repent of.
You can confess it.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can make restitution where appropriate.
You can begin repairing what your pride helped damage.
That is not weakness.
That is the fruit of grace.
And if you are the one who has been wounded, hear this carefully.
Forgiveness does not require you to call evil good.
It does not mean every unsafe relationship must immediately be restored.
It does not remove the need for truth, accountability, or wise boundaries.
And reconciliation, when possible, requires more than one person pretending nothing happened.
But in Christ, you are not required to let the sins of others define your worth forever.
The Lord sees what happened.
He knows the words that were spoken.
He knows how long you carried the shame.
He knows the difference between genuine guilt that calls for repentance and false guilt imposed by someone else's unreasonable demands.
And His invitation is not to remain imprisoned in either.
It is to come to Jesus.
The One who said:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (Matthew 11:28, KJV)
Maybe you are exhausted from trying to earn someone's approval.
Maybe you are tired of being judged by a mistake you made years ago.
Maybe you have spent so much of your life fearing rejection that you no longer know how to receive love.
Or maybe you are exhausted because you have been hiding from the truth about yourself.
The invitation of Christ reaches both the wounded and the guilty.
Come to Him.
Not to an imaginary Jesus who never confronts sin.
Not to a harsh caricature of God who delights in crushing people.
Come to the true Savior revealed in Scripture.
Full of grace and truth.
Holy and compassionate.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and receives those who turn to Him in faith.
The One who died and rose again.
The One who can transform what human pride has broken.
And perhaps that is the most important difference between Saul's throne and Christ's kingdom.
Saul's authority could become a weapon against the very people he was called to lead.
Jesus said of Himself:
"The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." (Mark 10:45, KJV)
In the Greek New Testament, the word translated "ransom" is λύτρον (lytron).
It refers to a ransom or price of release.
Jesus was not merely offering inspirational words about freedom.
He was describing the purpose of His sacrificial death.
He came to give His life for others.

And while the Hebrew verb used for Jonathan's rescue and the Greek noun used by Jesus belong to different languages and immediate contexts, both passages invite us to consider the seriousness of deliverance.
Jonathan was delivered from a threatened death.
Through Christ's sacrifice, sinners can be delivered from the condemnation their sins deserve.
The contrast is profound.
The people cried out that Jonathan should not die.
At Calvary, Jesus willingly died so that sinners could receive eternal life.
And on the third day, He rose again.
Death did not have the final word.
Sin did not have the final word.
The grave did not have the final word.
Jesus Christ is alive.
That is why our message is not simply about surviving painful circumstances.
It is about redemption.
It is about repentance.
It is about the God who takes sinners and makes them new through His Son.
It is about the Gospel that can reach into a family shattered by pride, a heart consumed by shame, a life marked by rebellion, or a soul weary from years of religious fear.
And declare that the story does not have to end where the wound began.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by denying the consequences of sin.
Not by promising that every earthly relationship will be repaired exactly as we desire.
But by bringing forgiveness, truth, new life, and everlasting hope through His finished work.
And that leaves us with one question we cannot afford to ignore.
What are we going to do with the truth we have just encountered?
Will we be like Saul, so committed to protecting our own position that we refuse correction?
Will we be like the silent bystander who recognizes harm but is afraid to speak?
Or will we respond with humility, courage, and faithfulness to God?
Perhaps you need to apologize to your child.
Perhaps you need to listen to your spouse without preparing your defense.
Perhaps you need to stop treating every disagreement as rebellion.
Perhaps you need to confront an injustice with wisdom and courage.
Perhaps you need to release the false belief that God despises you because someone in authority treated you harshly.
Or perhaps, for the first time, you need to surrender your life to Jesus Christ.
Not just admire Him.
Not just quote Him.
Not just follow Christian content while keeping your heart closed to His lordship.
But repent and trust Him.
Because the greatest tragedy would be to recognize Saul's pride in this story and refuse to recognize our own need for grace.
And the greatest victory would not be that this article moved your emotions for a few minutes.
It would be that the Word of God moved your heart toward Jesus.
If you need a prayer today, let it be this:

"Lord Jesus, search my heart. Expose the pride I have defended, the sins I have hidden, and the wounds I have allowed to shape my view of You. Forgive me where I have hurt others. Heal what is broken in me according to Your wisdom and will. Teach me to love truth more than my reputation, obedience more than control, and Your glory more than my own approval. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Help me turn from sin and follow You with a sincere heart. Amen."
And please, do not let this become another powerful story you read and forget.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list, there may be a parent who needs to learn the difference between godly authority and destructive control.
There may be a son or daughter still carrying wounds from words spoken years ago.
There may be a believer who has confused spiritual abuse with the character of God.
There may be someone who has become so hardened by pride that they desperately need the Holy Spirit to bring them to repentance.
Not because a post can save anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because God can use the truth of His Word, shared through ordinary people, to bring someone closer to the Savior.
And I want to invite you to do something more personal.
You do not need to reveal private details to strangers. But sometimes a simple, sincere confession of faith becomes the encouragement another struggling believer needs to see.
There is also a deeper way to stand with this mission.
And if you are looking for a meaningful way to glorify God through your resources, supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one expression of Christian generosity.
Scripture teaches us to honor the Lord with what He has entrusted to us, to support worthy ministry, and to give willingly.
Rather, you may choose to make it part of your voluntary monthly giving—an offering of support for the continuation and expansion of this Gospel-centered work.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Not a pressured giver.
Not a frightened giver.
A cheerful giver.
These resources can serve as daily reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share your faith with others.
Pray for this ministry.
Help place Scripture-centered encouragement in front of a person who might never have searched for it on their own.
Because the goal is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The goal is to make Jesus Christ known.
And I want to leave you with one final image.
A battlefield covered in the aftermath of victory.
A young man standing before his father.
A king determined that his own words must be upheld.
A people refusing to allow the son who had fought for them to be killed.
And then, the simple conclusion:
"He died not."
Jonathan walked away alive.
But centuries later, another Son would stand before human authorities, endure injustice, and willingly lay down His life.
No crowd could make His sacrifice unnecessary.
No human rescue could accomplish what He came to do.
He went to the cross.
He bore our sins.
He rose victorious.
And now the risen Christ calls sinners to come to Him, not to hide behind pride, fear, religious performance, or the wounds of yesterday.
So if you have been living under the weight of someone else's condemnation, bring your pain to Jesus.
If you have been making others suffer under the weight of your pride, bring your sin to Jesus.
If you have spent years trying to earn a love that human beings kept withholding, remember that God's grace is not purchased by your perfection.
And if you have never truly trusted Christ, today is an opportunity to turn to Him in repentance and faith.
Because the King you ultimately need is not one who demands that everyone else die to preserve His reputation.
He is the King who willingly died to save His people—and rose again to reign forever.
Saul was ready to lose his son rather than surrender his own words. Jesus surrendered His life so that sinners could be saved by God's grace.
